content: The guidelines for the prevention, care, and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis B infection, published in March 2015 by the World Health Organization (WHO), provide comprehensive recommendations for managing this condition. These guidelines address various aspects of hepatitis B, including prevention, diagnosis, and drug therapy, and are intended to guide healthcare professionals in delivering evidence-based care. The WHO emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material in this publication do not imply any opinion on the legal status of countries, territories, cities, or areas, nor on the delimitation of their boundaries. The mention of specific companies or products does not constitute endorsement or preference by the WHO. While every effort has been made to verify the information, the material is distributed without warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. The guidelines were developed with contributions from a diverse group of professionals, including clinicians, researchers, and public health experts. The Guidelines Development Group was chaired by Olufunmilayo Lesi (University of Lagos, Nigeria) and Brian McMahon (Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium, USA), with Nandi Siegfried (South African Cochrane Centre) serving as the methodologist. Experts from various countries and institutions provided input, including specialists in virology, hepatology, and public health. The document includes a glossary of terms to clarify key concepts. Acute hepatitis B infection is defined as a new-onset infection, diagnosed by the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and IgM antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc). Recovery is marked by the clearance of HBsAg and the development of antibodies to the hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs). Chronic hepatitis B infection is characterized by the persistence of HBsAg for six months or more after acute infection. The natural history of chronic hepatitis B includes several phases: 1. Immune-tolerant phase: This is an early stage of infection, often seen in individuals infected at birth or during early childhood, characterized by high viral replication. 2. Immune-active phase: This phase involves fluctuating levels of liver enzymes (aminotransferases) and high concentrations of HBV DNA. It may lead to seroconversion from hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) to anti-HBe. 3. Inactive phase (immune-control phase): This phase is marked by low viral replication, HBeAg negativity, anti-HBe positivity, normal alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, and HBV DNA concentrations below 2000 IU/mL. 4. HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B (immune-escape phase): This phase involves variable levels of HBV replication and liver injury, despite HBeAg negativity and anti-HBe positivity. Key serological markers include: HBsAg: Indicates active infection (acute or chronic). HBeAg: Associated with high levels of viral replication. Anti-HBs: Denotes immunity, either from vaccination or recovery from acute infection. Anti-HBe: Indicates seroconversion from HBeAg. Anti-HBc: Found in both acute and chronic infections, but not neutralizing. Advanced liver disease, such as cirrhosis, is characterized by extensive hepatic fibrosis, nodularity, and disrupted liver architecture. Decompensated cirrhosis presents with clinical complications, including jaundice, ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, sepsis, and renal failure. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a primary liver cancer arising from hepatocytes and is a potential complication of chronic hepatitis B. The guidelines also include recommendations for the prevention of hepatitis B transmission, particularly among high-risk populations, and strategies for monitoring and managing the disease. The development of these guidelines was supported by funding from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
